A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
self-efficacious students with high self-rating scores are more likely to achieve better grades in a psychology course.
self-efficacies are not enough to counter the limited knowledge and competence.

self-efficacious students with a high self-rating score are more likely to succeed in their academic endeavours than those who have a low self-rating score, irrespective of their self-efficaciousness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the self-efficacy beliefs of students in the sample were not strong enough to overcome the effects of their limited knowledge of the content of the course.
the relationship between self-efficacy (and other similar constructs) and academic achievement is not straightforward.
